This evaluation ran 11 chat-task evals (5 iterations each) comparing without_skill and with_skill on AWS Systems Manager/EC2 operations scenarios (disk-full plans, rpmdb corruption, dependency conflicts, Windows Update issues, etc.). One eval ("unrelated-question") was fully skipped because it was a should-not-trigger test, so no data exists there for either variant — that's absent data, not a failure.

Trigger firing: Both variants triggered the expected behavior 100% of the time across all 10 applicable evals — this dimension shows no difference and isn't informative for comparison.

Expected output / assertions: This is where the clearest and most consistent pattern emerges. In 8 of the 10 scored evals, with_skill met the expected output and passed its assertions at or near 100%, while without_skill's expected-output pass rate ranged from 0% to 80% (with several evals at a flat 0%, e.g. windows-disk-full-plan, rhel-dependency-conflict, ubuntu-inode-exhaustion, ubuntu-dpkg-lock, windows-cbs-corruption, windows-wuauserv-disabled). Almost every individual assertion that failed for without_skill (format requirements, naming the matching SOP, stating OS applicability, specific remediation details) passed consistently for with_skill, forming a strong "with_skill passes, without_skill fails" pattern across many separate assertions. A few assertions were flaky for without_skill (e.g., the rpmdb corruption "skip steps with reason" assertion, 40% for without_skill vs 100% for with_skill) or passed for both (e.g., "no Run Command document is sent" in no-matching-sop, and the SHA-2 root-cause tie-in in windows-2012r2-sha2), meaning those specific checks don't differentiate the variants or aren't yet discriminating well. Expected-output confidence was "medium" for without_skill's judgments versus "high" for with_skill's in nearly every eval, so the measurement of without_skill's shortfall itself carries somewhat less certainty than with_skill's near-perfect scores.

Quality comparisons (pairwise LLM judging on accuracy/actionability/completeness) present a more mixed picture, and many pairs were skipped (e.g., 4-5 of 5 pairs skipped in several evals, and all 5 skipped in windows-disk-full-plan and rhel-dependency-conflict), limiting how much can be concluded. Where pairs were evaluated, with_skill was favored more often in several evals (e.g., windows-cbs-corruption: 12 vs 3; rpmdb-corruption: 6 vs 3; ubuntu-inode-exhaustion and ubuntu-dpkg-lock: 6 vs 4 each), but without_skill was favored more often in others (no-matching-sop: 6 vs 1; windows-2012r2-sha2: 10 vs 5). Criterion-level splits show without_skill often favored on "accuracy" while with_skill is often favored on "actionability" and "completeness" — a tradeoff pattern rather than one-sided. All quality judgments carried medium average confidence, so these comparative quality findings should be treated as suggestive rather than definitive.

Runtime and cost: with_skill consistently ran much longer (roughly 20-50+ seconds vs without_skill's 0-15 seconds) and cost more per run (~$0.18-$0.44 vs ~$0.00-$0.13), with with_skill frequently exceeding the 30-second runtime threshold while without_skill rarely or never did. This is a substantial and consistent resource/time tradeoff associated with with_skill's higher expected-output and assertion pass rates — it is a tradeoff to weigh, not a standalone negative.

Output consistency across repeated runs: both variants were generally "consistent" to "mostly_consistent" (scores typically 2.33-3.0 out of 3) with high confidence, and neither showed sharp run-to-run instability. with_skill was "consistent" slightly more often (full 3.0 scores in about half the evals) while without_skill more often landed at "mostly_consistent," but the gap is modest.

Overall, the data shows a consistent, high-confidence pattern on expected-output/assertion metrics favoring with_skill, paired with substantially higher runtime and cost for with_skill, and a more mixed, lower-confidence picture on pairwise quality judgments where without_skill is sometimes favored (notably on accuracy) and many comparison pairs were skipped or unavailable.
